Multi-agent RL

With two learners, each one is part of the other's environment. As one adapts, the other's rewards change, so the world is no longer stationary and "the optimal policy" stops being a fixed target. The useful target becomes an equilibrium: a pair of policies where neither player gains by changing alone.

The maths

Rock-paper-scissors is a two-player zero-sum game. With actions ordered rock, paper, scissors, player 1's payoff matrix is

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$

Row $i$ is player 1's move, column $j$ player 2's, and player 2 gets $-A_{ij}$. With mixed strategies (probability vectors) $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$, player 1's expected payoff is

$$\mathbf x^\top A\, \mathbf y = \sum_{i,j} x_i A_{ij}\, y_j$$

The vector $A\mathbf y$ holds the payoff of each pure move against $\mathbf y$. A best response plays the largest entry. That is all the agent in the first part does, with $\mathbf y$ estimated from your counts.

A pair $(\mathbf x^*, \mathbf y^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium if neither player can gain by deviating alone:

$$\mathbf x^\top A\, \mathbf y^* \le \mathbf x^{*\top} A\, \mathbf y^* \le \mathbf x^{*\top} A\, \mathbf y \quad \text{for all } \mathbf x, \mathbf y$$

For rock-paper-scissors it is $\mathbf x^* = \mathbf y^* = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$, with value 0. Against the uniform mix every move earns exactly 0, so nothing can exploit it. How far a strategy is from equilibrium is measured by its exploitability, the most a best-responding opponent can win against it: $\max_j\, (-\mathbf x^\top A)_j$.

Policy gradient with a softmax policy $x_k \propto e^{\theta_k}$ (Lesson 70) moves each logit by

$$\frac{\partial\, \mathbf x^\top A \mathbf y}{\partial \theta_k} = x_k \big( (A\mathbf y)_k - \mathbf x^\top A \mathbf y \big)$$

Each player climbs its own gradient while the other moves. The pair circles the equilibrium instead of converging to it, and with finite steps the circles slowly widen. The running averages still approach $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$, as the exploitability counter shows. This matches a general result: in two-player zero-sum games, if both players have vanishing average regret (multiplicative-weights learners do, for example), their average strategies converge to a Nash equilibrium. Fictitious play (each plays a best response to the other's average) also converges in average (Robinson, 1951). Self-play in AlphaZero (Lesson 96) relies on the same zero-sum structure.
